content: Salmeterol, when used for asthma, has been associated with an increased risk of severe or fatal asthma-related complications, as observed in a large clinical study. Patients with asthma who used salmeterol experienced a higher mortality rate due to asthma problems compared to those who did not use the medication. If you have asthma, using salmeterol may elevate the likelihood of experiencing serious or life-threatening asthma complications. Your doctor will only prescribe salmeterol if other medications have failed to adequately control your asthma or if your asthma is so severe that it requires the use of two medications for proper management. Salmeterol should not be the first or sole medication used to treat asthma. It is not suitable for rapidly worsening asthma. Inform your doctor if you have had frequent severe asthma attacks or if you have ever been hospitalized due to asthma symptoms. If you notice any signs of worsening asthma, contact your doctor immediately. These signs include: Reduced effectiveness of your short-acting inhaler compared to previous use. Increased need for puffs or more frequent use of your short-acting inhaler. Using four or more puffs per day of your short-acting inhaler for two or more consecutive days. Using more than one canister (200 inhalations) of your short-acting inhaler within an 8-week period. Worsening results on your peak flow meter, a device used to monitor breathing. Needing emergency room treatment for asthma. No improvement in symptoms after using salmeterol regularly for one week or worsening symptoms at any point during treatment. Discuss the risks of using salmeterol with your doctor. You will receive a Medication Guide from your doctor or pharmacist when starting salmeterol and with each prescription refill. Read this information carefully and ask your healthcare provider any questions you may have. You can also access the Medication Guide on the FDA website or the manufacturer’s website. Salmeterol is prescribed to treat wheezing, shortness of breath, and breathing difficulties caused by asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which includes chronic bronchitis and emphysema. It is also used to prevent exercise-induced bronchospasm. Salmeterol belongs to a class of medications called long-acting beta agonists (LABAs). It works by relaxing and opening the airways in the lungs, making breathing easier. Salmeterol is available as a dry powder for oral inhalation using a specially designed inhaler. For asthma or COPD, it is typically used twice daily, in the morning and evening, approximately 12 hours apart. Use it at the same times each day. To prevent exercise-induced breathing difficulties, use it at least 30 minutes before exercise, but not more than once every 12 hours. If you are already using salmeterol twice daily, do not take an additional dose before exercising. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully. Use salmeterol exactly as directed. Do not use more or less of it or use it more frequently than prescribed. Consult your doctor about how to use other oral or inhaled asthma medications during your treatment with salmeterol. If you were taking a corticosteroid to prevent airway swelling, your doctor will likely advise you to continue using it as before. If you were using a short-acting beta agonist inhaler like albuterol regularly, your doctor may instruct you to stop regular use but continue using it for sudden asthma symptoms. Do not change your medication regimen without consulting your doctor. Do not use salmeterol during an asthma or COPD attack. Your doctor will prescribe a short-acting inhaler for use during such attacks. Salmeterol helps control symptoms of asthma and other lung diseases but does not cure them. Do not stop using salmeterol without consulting your doctor, as sudden discontinuation may worsen your symptoms. Before using the salmeterol inhaler for the first time, ask your doctor, pharmacist, or respiratory therapist to demonstrate its use. Practice using the inhaler under their supervision. Follow these steps to use the inhaler: 1. If using a new inhaler, remove it from the box and foil wrapper. Write the date you opened the pouch and the replacement date (6 weeks later) on the inhaler label. 2. Hold the inhaler in one hand and place the thumb of your other hand on the thumb grip. Push your thumb away from you until the mouthpiece appears and snaps into position. 3. Hold the inhaler horizontally with the mouthpiece facing you. Slide the lever away from you until it clicks. Each time the lever is pushed back, a dose is ready for inhalation, and the dose counter will decrease. Avoid wasting doses by mishandling the lever or tilting the inhaler. 4. Hold the inhaler level and away from your mouth. Exhale as far as is comfortable. 5. Keep the inhaler flat and place the mouthpiece to your lips. Inhale quickly and deeply through the inhaler, not through your nose. 6. Remove the inhaler from your mouth and hold your breath for 10 seconds or as long as is comfortable. Exhale slowly. 7. You may taste or feel the salmeterol powder. Do not inhale another dose even if you do not taste or feel it. If unsure, contact your doctor or pharmacist. 8. Slide the thumb grip back toward you until the device clicks shut. Do not exhale into the inhaler, disassemble it, or wash any part of it. Keep the inhaler dry and do not use it with a spacer. Salmeterol may be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before using salmeterol, inform your doctor if you are allergic to salmeterol, other medications, milk protein, or any foods. Notify your doctor if you are using another LABA, such as fluticasone-salmeterol (Advair) or formoterol (Foradil). Your doctor will advise which medication to use and which to discontinue. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Mention beta blockers, diuretics, asthma or COPD medications, antidepressants, and monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs). Your doctor may adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have or have had irregular heartbeat, high blood pressure, hyperthyroidism, diabetes, seizures, or liver or heart disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor. If you become pregnant while using salmeterol, contact your doctor. Continue your normal diet unless otherwise instructed by your doctor. If you miss a dose, skip it and resume your regular schedule. Do not inhale a double dose to compensate for a missed one. Salmeterol may cause side effects. Notify your doctor if you experience severe or persistent symptoms such as uncontrollable shaking, headache, nervousness, dizziness, cough, nasal congestion, ear pain, pale skin, muscle pain or cramps, sore throat, throat irritation, flu-like symptoms, nausea, heartburn, tooth pain, dry mouth, mouth sores, red or irritated eyes, difficulty sleeping, or tingling in the hands or feet. Serious side effects require immediate medical attention. These include coughing, wheezing, or chest tightness after inhalation; rapid or pounding heartbeat; chest pain; rash; hives; swelling of the face, throat, tongue, lips, or extremities; hoarseness; choking; difficulty swallowing; or high-pitched breathing. Report any unusual problems to your doctor. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch program. Store salmeterol in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Discard the inhaler 6 weeks after opening or when the dose indicator reads 0, whichever comes first. Consult your pharmacist for proper disposal. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222 or call 911 if the victim collapses or is not breathing. Symptoms of overdose include seizures, chest pain, dizziness, fainting, blurred vision, rapid or irregular heartbeat, nervousness, headache, uncontrollable shaking, muscle cramps, dry mouth, nausea, fatigue, or difficulty sleeping. Keep all appointments with your doctor. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist for questions about refilling your prescription.
